adds.title: LGBT rights in Nigeria - Wikipedia
adds.summary: Wikipedia's Nigeria LGBT-rights overview records that same-sex sexual activity has been illegal across the country since 1916 and that the Same-Sex Marriage (Prohibition) Act — passed by the House of Representatives on 30 May 2013 and signed into law by President Goodluck Jonathan in January 2014 — criminalises all forms of same-sex unions, punishing them with up to 14 years' imprisonment. It states the death penalty is confined to the twelve northern states operating Shari'a-based criminal codes and that in the southern portion of the country a life sentence is the maximum. The page also records no legal recognition of gender identity, no anti-discrimination protections and no recognition of same-sex relationships. Ondo is not named on the page, but as a southern state it stands under the secular national 14-year framework, matching this record's position that no state-specific protective statute or enforcement divergence is documented.

adds.title: Country policy and information note: sexual orientation, gender identity and expression, and sex characteristics, Nigeria, June 2025 (accessible) - GOV.UK
adds.summary: The UK Home Office's June 2025 country policy and information note documents the national criminal framework that applies across all states, including the 2014 statute punishing same-sex unions, and records countrywide harm patterns of arrests, detention and mob violence against LGBT+ people. It confirms that the twelve northern states' Shari'a penal codes — with penalties up to death by stoning — remain in force, so the death-penalty layer does not extend to Ondo, and quotes Section 217 of the Criminal Code under which any male committing or procuring an act of gross indecency with another male, in public or private, is guilty of a felony liable to three years' imprisonment. It cites Victor Oluwasina Ayeni, senior lecturer in law at Adekunle Ajasin University in Ondo state, observing in a January 2017 book chapter that the Code fails to define what constitutes an act of gross indecency. This confirms the national framework — including the gross-indecency offence applicable in southern states such as Ondo — and the absence of any documented state-specific divergence.

adds.title: LGBT rights in Nigeria - Wikipedia
adds.summary: Wikipedia's Nigeria LGBT-rights overview records that same-sex sexual activity has been illegal across the country since 1916 and that the Same-Sex Marriage (Prohibition) Act — passed by the House of Representatives on 30 May 2013 and signed into law in January 2014 — criminalises all forms of same-sex unions, with up to 14 years' imprisonment as the maximum federal penalty and the death penalty confined to the twelve northern Shari'a states. The page is anchored to Delta specifically: it records that in June 2018 Nigerian police arrested more than 100 party-goers at a hotel in Asaba, Delta State, on charges that they were gays and lesbians and that by July 2018 they were facing homosexuality-related charges in court, and that in August 2023 police raided a gay wedding in Warri, Delta state, arresting dozens in the case known as the 'Warri 67', of whom 67 were charged to court following a mass arrest at a party or marriage ceremony. It also records nationwide patterns of arrests, raids and vigilante violence relevant to a traveller in Delta. This is the national-framework source for the record's claims that the 2014 statute punishes same-sex unions with up to 14 years' imprisonment and that no state-specific protective statute exists.

adds.title: Country policy and information note: sexual orientation, gender identity and expression, and sex characteristics, Nigeria, June 2025 (accessible) - GOV.UK
adds.summary: The UK Home Office's June 2025 country policy and information note documents the national criminal framework that applies across all states, including the 2014 statute punishing same-sex unions with up to 14 years' imprisonment and Section 217 of the Criminal Code making male gross indecency a felony liable to three years' imprisonment, with the death penalty confined to the twelve northern Shari'a states. It cites the USSD 2023 human rights report recording that on 27 August 2023 police in Delta State raided a 'white party' organized by the LGBTQI+ community and detained more than 200 individuals, with police alleging the event was a same-sex wedding while some civil society representatives disputed that account. It also quotes a human rights lawyer based in Warri, Delta state, on 'kito' (predatory same-sex assault) victims under-reporting for fear of prosecution. This confirms the national framework under which Delta stands and documents the recorded Delta-specific enforcement incidents underlying this record's position that state-level documentation is thin rather than demonstrating safety.

adds.title: Police arrest 67 gay suspects in Delta hotel - Daily Post Nigeria
adds.summary: Daily Post reports that police officers from Ekpan Division in Uvwie Local Government Area of Delta State arrested 67 suspects on 27 August 2023 at 9 pm at Teebolus Hotel, Refinery Road, Ekpan, for allegedly conducting and attending a same-sex wedding ceremony between Daniel Pius (the groom), 22, and Maxwel Ohwonohwo (the bride), 20. Delta State Police Command spokesman DSP Bright Edafe said the raid followed a male cross-dresser's confession that he was a member of a gay club travelling to a gay marriage ceremony, that the suspects fled on the officers' arrival but 67 were chased and arrested, and that drugs and 'gay marriage ceremonial dresses' were recovered. Edafe said the suspects and exhibits were in custody and efforts continued to arrest fleeing members for possible prosecution, and that one suspect alleged he was sexually assaulted by a man at the hotel while intoxicated. This is a direct, dated, on-the-ground record of enforcement action inside Delta State (Warri), evidencing that the national anti-LGBT framework is actively enforced in this jurisdiction and that incidents are frequently framed together with drug allegations.
